title: Inventory Accounting and Costing
overview: Inventory plays a critical role in the financial health of any business, whether in trading, manufacturing, contracting, or service industries. Its impact extends across the income statement and balance sheet. This course provides a step-by-step guide to best practices in managing inventory, from the purchasing process to cost allocation, while exploring cost flow assumptions like FIFO, LIFO, and weighted average. Participants will also learn how to ensure accurate inventory valuations, reflect net realizable value, and use tools such as Excel and pivot tables for analysis and calculations.
audience: Inventory professionals, including supervisors, account managers, and purchasing coordinators.
New employees involved in inventory handling.
Operations managers seeking to enhance their inventory accounting expertise.
methodology: This interactive course combines brief expert-led presentations, group exercises, and practical case studies. Participants will apply their learning using Excel and present their results to enhance understanding and collaboration.
competencies: Applying professional judgment for special cases.
Utilizing Excel and pivot tables for data analysis.
objectivesIntro: By the end of the course, participants will be able to:
objectives: Identify different inventory types and construct a complete inventory cycle, from purchasing to sales.
Differentiate between perpetual and periodic inventory methods and evaluate various cost allocation techniques.
Accurately measure and account for inventory in line with IFRS and GAAP standards.
Understand the impact of inventory accounting policies on financial statements, including write-downs and write-backs.
Apply professional judgment in accounting for inventory not physically on hand.
Analyze the effects of different cost flow assumptions on financial statements and income.
Utilize Excel and pivot tables to analyze inventory balances and calculate weighted average costs.

items.text: Role of inventory within current assets.
The four primary reasons for maintaining inventory.
Inventory types across industries: merchandise, manufacturing, construction, and real estate.
Distinguishing inventory from fixed assets and investment properties.
Comparing perpetual and periodic inventory systems.
Differences between cost accounting and financial accounting.
Direct material, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead.
Costs of purchase and conversion, including rebates and discounts.
Market price determination under the Lower of Cost or Market (LCM) method (GAAP).
Handling slow-moving and obsolete inventory: write-downs and write-backs.
Accounting for errors during physical inventory counts.
Accounting for inventory not physically on hand:
Inventory sold with rights of return or subject to installation and inspection.
Impact of inventory accounting policy changes on financial statements.
Key inventory disclosures required by IFRS and GAAP.
Weighted average and moving average methods.
